web_evidence.title: Excerpt from Blessings by Anna Quindlen
web_evidence.note: A sustained two-page Chapter One extract, reproduced by permission of Random House, narrates the couple, Lydia, and the estate externally as he, she, and they, with no participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: Blessings by Anna Quindlen
web_evidence.note: The publisher's author interview establishes that the novel alternates the focal perspectives of Lydia Blessing and Skip Cuddy as two ways of telling the same story. Both focal strands appear in third person in the supplied quotations and excerpts, so this is focal alternation rather than person alternation.

web_evidence.title: Blessings by Anna Quindlen
web_evidence.note: An interior extract narrates Lydia watching Skip as she and he and reports what she thinks, corroborating third-person narration beyond the opening.

web_evidence.title: All in the Family
web_evidence.note: The contemporary review describes Quindlen's whole-book method as interweaving Skip's present story with Lydia's memories; this matches the two third-person focal strands found in the prose evidence.

web_evidence.title: Review of Blessings by wolfiegrrrl
web_evidence.note: A low-tier reader account explicitly identifies an omniscient narrator and discusses that narration across the completed book; it is corroborative rather than controlling evidence.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and narrates in third person, moving through the perspectives and memories of Lydia Blessing and Skip Cuddy. The quotations repeatedly show third-person free-indirect access to both focal characters, while the authorized opening independently presents the story in third person and an interior extract corroborates that pattern. The publisher's interview confirms that Lydia and Skip alternate as focal perspectives, not as different grammatical-person narrators. Generic you in q00060, dialogue in q00064, and the two gnomic quotations do not alter the base person. No credible evidence of sustained first- or second-person sections was found; the only minor limitation is that the strongest authorized prose source covers the opening rather than the entire novel.
